top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits one well-bounded achievement: transparent, replicated empirical designs showing how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, job polarisation and local labour-market adjustment. The work is mature, spanning the early 1990s to the mid-2010s. The core finding of large, persistent local adjustment costs has survived more than a decade of re-analysis, and only the magnitudes are debated. Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers, and Autor and Dorn (2013) carries the polarisation strand, so the citation can span both strands without claiming the task theory of Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo. It also avoids the closer marginal-credit overlap of Katz's education-and-technology work with the 2023 prize. P002 (Katz in place of Dorn) is nearly as strong, because Katz anchors the older skill-premium evidence, and the choice between them is a definitional one. P003 has a compact core, but it carries unresolved priority claims (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and contested welfare-gain magnitudes. P004 is a credible methods contribution with clean attribution, but its reach is narrower and the Bresnahan question is open. All four proposals are mature and worthy enough to rank above no award.
recusal_note: No connection to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Helpman, Melitz, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from the profile. Documented ties are to committee colleagues: IIES colleagues Krusell and Boppart, co-authorship with Boppart and Friberg, and frequent co-authorship with Krusell. None of them is a credited name on any proposal. Krusell's work on technology and wage inequality is field-adjacent to B009 only. Disclosed and not adjudicated, and no independent verification is claimed.
